article.headline: Three Tiers of Understanding Found Inside Language Models
article.lede: A paper published in *Philosophical Studies* by Pierre Beckmann of EPFL and philosopher Matthieu Queloz of the University of Bern argues that the mechanistic interpretability literature — the emerging effort to reverse-engineer the internal computations of neural networks — has quietly accumulated enough empirical evidence to challenge the claim that large language models merely imitate text. Their argument is not that LLMs understand as humans do; it is that the binary question is the wrong one. In its place they propose a three-tier framework, grounded in specific experimental findings, for mapping what LLMs actually do internally.
article.body:
The paper, posted to arXiv in July 2025 and peer-reviewed into *Philosophical Studies* in 2026, builds from a philosophically standard account of understanding as “apprehending relational structure” — grasping how parts hang together — rather than merely accumulating propositions. From that foundation, Beckmann and Queloz derive three tiers, each tied to a specific type of internal organization that **mechanistic interpretability** (MI, the subfield that reverse-engineers neural networks rather than treating them as black boxes) has actually demonstrated inside deployed models.

The first tier is *conceptual understanding*, defined as tracking the same entity or property across wildly varied surface forms. The evidence comes from Anthropic's 2024 “Scaling Monosemanticity” work, which used *sparse autoencoders* — tools that decompose the dense, overlapping representations inside a network into cleaner, more separable features — to extract 34 million interpretable features from Claude 3 Sonnet. A single feature for the Golden Gate Bridge fired whether the model encountered the phrase in prose, an image description, or ASCII art rendering of the bridge. This is not a lookup; it is an internal direction in *latent space* (the high-dimensional vector space of a model's activations) that unifies diverse presentations under one representation — precisely the cognitive operation at the heart of concept formation.

The second tier, *state-of-the-world understanding*, requires not just stable concepts but dynamic tracking of contingent facts. The paradigm case is Othello-GPT (Li et al., 2023): a transformer trained only on sequences of legal Othello moves, given no board descriptions, developed a nonlinear internal model of board state accurate to 98.3 percent across all 64 squares. Crucially, causal-intervention experiments — directly patching the model's representation of a specific square's occupancy — changed its predictions in the expected direction, ruling out mere surface-level statistical correlation and confirming the representation was doing genuine computational work.

**Principled understanding**, the third tier, is the most philosophically demanding. It requires the model to cease relying on memorized facts and discover a compact rule that *unifies* a range of cases. The clearest evidence is the “grokking” phenomenon (Nanda et al., 2023): small transformers trained on modular arithmetic first memorize training examples, then — after a period of apparent stagnation — abruptly generalize by discovering an algorithm built from discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities. The *circuit* that emerges — a localized subgraph of attention heads and MLP layers that causally drives the behavior — derives answers from a principle rather than a table. The same pattern appears in induction heads: a two-component attention *circuit* that generalizes the rule “if you saw token A followed by B before, and you see A again, predict B” to arbitrary token pairs.

The paper's most important caveat is what the authors call “parallel heterogeneous mechanisms”: a single model can deploy all three tiers simultaneously and inconsistently. A circuit implementing principled understanding of modular arithmetic may coexist with brute-force memorization of unrelated facts in the same weight matrix. This architectural divergence from human cognition — where higher-order understanding tends to globally displace lower-order heuristics — makes simple equivalence claims untenable in either direction. Beckmann and Queloz's prescription is *comparative epistemology*: not “does the model understand?” but “in what respects, and by what mechanisms, does its understanding resemble or diverge from our own?” The *stochastic-parrots* thesis — the influential 2021 argument by Bender et al. that LLMs process linguistic form without semantic content — is the paper's explicit foil; the authors argue MI evidence renders that picture increasingly untenable, while stopping well short of claiming human-equivalent cognition.

concepts.definition: A subfield of AI safety and interpretability research that aims to reverse-engineer the internal computations of neural networks — identifying what specific neurons, attention heads, and MLP layers actually compute, and why. Rather than treating a model as a black box and measuring only input-output behavior, MI researchers trace causally active circuits responsible for specific behaviors using ablation and activation patching.

A neural network tool used in mechanistic interpretability to decompose the dense, overlapping representations inside a large model into cleaner individual features. It enforces sparsity — at any moment, only a small fraction of features are active — which tends to separate concepts that are otherwise tangled together in the same neurons, revealing interpretable directions in the model's latent space.

The high-dimensional vector space of internal activations inside a neural network. A model's representation of a concept corresponds to a specific direction or region in this space. The linear representation hypothesis — supported by work on word embeddings and Anthropic's feature extraction — holds that meaningful features are encoded as linear directions (vectors), making them in principle discoverable through linear algebra.

In mechanistic interpretability, a circuit is a localized, causally active subgraph of components — specific attention heads, MLP layers, or neurons — that together implement a particular behavior. Circuits are identified by ablation (disabling components to see what breaks) and activation patching (swapping in representations from different inputs) to confirm they causally drive the output rather than merely correlating with it.

A training phenomenon in which a neural network first memorizes its training data and achieves near-zero training loss, then — after a substantial delay with no apparent progress — suddenly generalizes to a compact algorithm that works on held-out data. Named by Power et al. (2022) and reverse-engineered by Nanda et al. (2023), grokking is the strongest current evidence that models can transition from rote memorization to principled rule-based reasoning.

A term coined in a 2021 paper by Bender, Gebru, and colleagues to characterize large language models as systems that stochastically sample plausible-sounding text from learned probability distributions, without any genuine semantic understanding. The thesis holds that text-only training cannot ground meaning, because meaning requires embodied, social experience — a position Beckmann and Queloz argue is empirically undercut by mechanistic interpretability evidence.

A two-component attention-head circuit identified in transformer models that implements in-context learning: if the model has seen token A followed by token B anywhere earlier in the sequence, and encounters A again, the induction circuit boosts the probability of B. Identified by Elhage et al. (2021) at Anthropic, induction heads are a paradigm example of a compact circuit implementing a general rule rather than a memorized fact.

An approach proposed by Beckmann and Queloz that replaces the binary question “does the AI understand?” with a finer-grained comparative question: “in what respects, and by what mechanisms, does AI understanding resemble or diverge from human understanding?” It treats LLMs as a new epistemic kind rather than a deficient imitation of the human mind, and uses mechanistic evidence to map the similarities and differences empirically.
